niṣeka
It is the same as गर्भाधान (‘inseminating’), one of the sixteen सṁस्कारस्.
------------------------------------------
See ṢOḌAŚASAṀSKĀRAS.

niṣkramaṇa
(‘going out,’ ‘taking [the baby] outside the होउसे’)
------------------------------------------
The entire life of a Hindu is closely connected with religious rites and cere-monies, in some form or the other. The षोडश-सṁस्कारस् (sixteen sacraments) reflect this basic attitude.
The निष्क्रमण (or उपनिष्क्रमण) is one of the minor सṁस्कारस् and is performed by taking the new-born baby out of the होउसे in the open and exposing it to the sunlight. It may be done either on the twelfth day or in the fourth month.
Worshipping the sun by the ड़थेर् of the baby with an offering prepared out of milk and presenting the baby to the sun with some Vedic mantras (Ṛgveda 1.50.1) is an important part of this ritual.
Some गृह्यसूत्रस् prescribe the performance of a होम also.
In some works like those of गोभिल and Khādira, only candradarśana (showing the मोओन् on a full-मोओन् day) to the baby is mentioned.

niṣka
------------------------------------------
Using coins as money was not unknown in ancient India. Suvarṇa, śatamāna and निष्क are some of the words used to indicate these.
The word ‘niṣka’ occurs in the Atharvaveda (5.14.3) and refers to a necklace of निष्क (may be a gold-coin or a thin plate of gold).
The Ṛgveda (2.33.10) refers to रुद्र as wearing a ‘Viśvarūpaniṣka’ (golden pieces stamped with various figures).
The following table can give an idea of the निष्क by weight:
Weight of 5 liquorice seeds = 1 māṣa
16 māṣas = 1 suvarṇa
108 suvarṇas = 1 निष्क.
‘Dīnāra’ seems to be another name used for निष्क.

niṣedha
(‘prohibition’)
------------------------------------------
Vidhis (injunctions) and niṣedhas or pratiṣedhas (prohibitions) are common in Vedic rituals. They are also seen in the धर्मशास्त्रस्.
If a विधि ordains a person to do something which will benefit him, a निषेध prohibits him from doing something which will harm him. Such niṣedhas are indicated by the negative particle ‘nañ’.
For instance: ‘na anṛtaṁ vadet, na māṁsam aśnīyāt,’ ‘One should not speak what is false, nor eat flesh’ (Taittirīya Saṁhitā 2.5.5.6).
Here uttering falsehood and eating flesh have been prohibited.
In the dharmaśāstra works, the particle ‘nañ’ (‘not’) is used in the sense of paryudāsa or exception. For instance, a स्नातक (one who has just finished Vedic studies) should not say anything to another which hurts him unless there is a specific reason. It does not altogether prohibit speaking an unpleasant thing, if and when necessary, as in the case of a parent chastising an erring son.
In some cases there may be two negatives or niṣedhas opposed to each other causing confusion. Then one has the choice to accept one and reject the other subject to certain conditions.

niṣādasthapati
------------------------------------------
Every society has its own rules to regulate the lives of its members both at the personal and at the social levels. As the society evolves in its civilisation and culture, these rules also, often, undergo change.
Evolution of yajñas and yāgas (Vedic sacrifices) gradually needed the involvement of more and more people including those from the lower varṇas or castes. In return for their valuable services, some of them like the rathakāras and niṣādas, had to be accorded certain privileges.
So, in course of time, the rathakāras (‘makers of chariots,’ the carpenters) and the निषादस्थपति (chieftain of the niṣādas) were given the privilege of undergoing the sacrament of उपनयन and keeping the Vedic fires in which they could offer oblations. They were permitted to perform Raudraiṣṭi, अग्निहोत्र and the दर्शपूर्णमास sacrifices (vide Satyāṣāḍha Kalpasūtras 3.1).

niṣāda
(‘one who sits [or lives on the outskirts of a village]’)
------------------------------------------
Though the fourfold division of the Hindu society, designated as the वर्ण-system, is very ancient, mixing up of the varṇas (varṇasaṅkara) either within the ambit of the sacrament of मर्रिअगे or outside it, was a real and continuing phenomenon. This gave rise to many new castes and subcastes. The निषाद is one such.
Niṣādas were the offsprings of a ब्राह्मण male from a śūdra woman. They were considered to be outside the pale of the four castes.
They are often described as dark in colour with reddish eyes and living by hunting wild animals.
The Rāmāyaṇa (Ayodhyākāṇḍa 50.33; 52.77-92) mentions that गुह who was the chieftain of the niṣādas, helped राम to cross the गङ्गा river. Later he took भरत to meet राम (ibid 89.12-19).
In मुसिच्, निषाद (ni) is the seventh note. It is supposed to come out of the region of lalāṭa (forehead) and resemble the sound of an elephant.

niśśreyas
(‘highest good’)
------------------------------------------
The Kaṭha Upaniṣad (2.2) declares that every human being has the opportunity to choose between the प्रेयस् and the श्रेयस्.
Preyas is what is pleasant, the apparently good, but which ultimately turns out to be bad, painful and ruinous.
Śreyas is that which is really good, though at first sight, it may not appear to be attractive.
A wise person always chooses the latter in preference to the former.
Śreyas, again, has two stages: the अभ्युदय and the निश्श्रेयस्. The former is worldly well-being got through धर्म or the righteous means. This, however, is not permanent.
Niśśreyas, on the other hand, is spiritual well-being, leading to मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्, the highest good. The word is used to indicate मोक्ष also.

niṣpatti-avasthā
(‘state of consummation [of प्राणायाम]’)
------------------------------------------
Prāṇāyāma is a part of yogic practices. It helps in controlling the मिन्द् and restoring the हुमोउर्स् to a balanced state to regain health, by a systematic control of breath.
It has four states out of which the निष्पत्ति-अवस्था is the last. It is the consummation of प्राणायाम coinciding with the जीवन्मुक्ति state.
The actual methods have to be learnt from a competent teacher.
See also PRĀṆĀYĀMA.
